messages.subject: Re: spotlight surveys => responsive movement bias
messages.body_plain:
Dear Colleagues,

sorry for cross-posting and for the follow up, but for the method mentioned
below and when DISTANCE Sampling would be applied, I wonder how these could
deal with the responsive movement bias, e.g. when spot-lighting is done and
when cars driving on gravel roads are used.

We know the expected frequency distribution before disturbance and
afterwards (from DISTANCE); could that be used to correct abundances and
still obtain
decent abundance estimates with confidence? The responsive movement I am
dealing with is basically just a consistent distance offset by app. 50m
(short distance escape/avoidance).

Thanks very much for any advice; it's a key question for us.

Kind regards

    F.

Subject: Re: spotlight surveys

Jeff- Spotlighting off-road has been done by black-footed ferret biologists
at night for years. It could likely be applied to any nocturnal furbearer
that could be approached within a few hundred meters at night.  We did this
with deep cycling marine 12 v. batteries on backpack frames, using hand-held
spotlights (candlepower will depend on how far you need to project a light
source with respect to terrain, vegetation, etc.).  We picked up coyotes,
badgers and porcupines on a regular basis. The deep cycling rechargable
marine batteries were good for an entire night (8+ hours) of continuous
operation.  Hope this helps.

Hi,

assuming that many locations of the world have received DISTANCE Sampling
surveys,
I am wondering if there have been approaches that connect and store such
results
in centralised databases (not the field data, but the DISTANCE Sampling
analysis results, or at least geo-referenced density estimates + SD +
detection details?

There are approaches such as SPECIESANALYST/DIGGER etc. which deal with
presence/absence (point based),
but I wonder if there are specific approaches/efforts that can or will
handle
DISTANCE Sampling (abundance) data, e.g. line transects, and databases
connected and for download via the WWW ?

I assume there is a general survey design, as well as a spatial
(coordinates), effort (how many surveys) and mapping (=GIS) issue in such
databases, too ?

I briefly heard of ABCD, would that be the only approach, so far ?

Thanks very much for any information; best regards

Centre for Research into Ecological and Environmental Modelling
University of St Andrews
St Andrews, Scotland

Announcement:
Short Course on Estimating Animal Abundance
2nd - 6th September 2003

Have you ever struggled to make sense of the various methods
for estimating animal abundance? Plot sampling, distance sampling,
 removal methods, catch-effort, change-in-ratio, mark-recapture...
Or are you familiar with some of the methods and want to know
more about the others?

This course will teach the concepts underlying all the main
abundance estimation methods in a rigorous but accessible way.
We cover methods from quadrant sampling of closed, static
populations to state-space modelling methods for open, dynamic
populations. The material is designed primarily for life- and
environmental scientists, wildlife managers and conservation
workers, but it may also be of interest to applied statisticians
working in these fields. Participants will need to have some
numerical training (an undergraduate-level course in statistics,
for example) although the key statistical concepts required will
be developed in the early part of the course. A maximum of 30
participants can be accommodated.

Funding for the course has come from the UK research councils,
enabling us to charge very modest registration fees.  In addition,
the councils have provided funding to cover reasonable
accommodation and subsistence expenses for up to ten attendees
who are EPSRC or NERC PhD students.

For more information, see
http://www.creem.st-and.ac.uk/conferences.php

**********************************************************
ANNOUNCEMENT
**********************************************************

DISTANCE WORKSHOPS 2003
Centre for Research into Ecological and Environmental Modelling
University of St Andrews
St Andrews, Scotland

The aim of these workshops is to train participants in the latest
methods for design and analysis of distance sampling surveys,
including line and point transects. The workshops are taught by
leading researchers in the field, using Distance software.

*********************************************************

Workshop 1: Introduction to Distance Sampling, 10-12 September
An introductory workshop focusing on standard distance sampling
methods. The workshop will be a blend of theory and practice and
participants will learn how to use version 4 of the program
Distance. Participants will gain a solid grounding in both
survey design and methods of analysis for distance sampling
surveys.

**********************************************************

Workshop 2: Advanced Techniques and Recent Developments in Distance
Sampling,
15-17 September
A workshop designed for those who are already familiar with the
basics, where we will teach advanced material such as automated
survey design, adaptive sampling, incorporating covariates into
the detection function, methods for where g(0)<1, and spatial
modelling of density. Participants will learn the more advanced
features of version 4 of Distance.

**********************************************************

For both workshops, participants are encouraged to bring their
own data sets, and can expect to do some preliminary analyses of
their data.

The number of participants on both workshops is strictly limited,
and for this reason we encourage you to register as soon as
possible. Information and forms can be downloaded from our web

messages.subject: Re: Using stratum area
messages.body_plain:
> > Please could anyone tell me if Distance 4.0 can produce

> > "better" estimates if an area is specified for each stratum?  How does
> > the prgramme make an estimate of density without an area entered?

Distance sampling is a form of plot sampling, but with uncertain
detection on the plots.  We know plot area, so if we can estimate
probability of detection, we have an estimate of the effective area
surveyed.  Estimated density is then number of animals detected over
effective area surveyed.  So you don't need to know the size of the wider
area that the plots represent.

Distance only uses size of the survey region to convert estimates of
animal density to estimates of animal abundance.

Steve Buckland

messages.subject_clean: zero encounter rate, use of neg exponential model
messages.body_plain:
Dear List,

I'd like to ask for some help with Distance 4.0 release 2.
First,in "Introduction to Distance Sampling", section 2.4, p. 48, it states
the "exponential + simple polynomial is available ..for salvage analysis..".
The authors further state this model should only be used in unusual
circumstances. However, the negative exponential model fits my data best
(using delta AIC). Neg-exp model AIC is 2885.69, with one parameter. Next
best is the half-normal model, AIC 2890.20, two parameters. Then is the
uniform model with AIC 2890.22, two parameters. Density estimates between
the neg-exp and next best fitting half-normal model differ by ~20%, so this
is no small decision. Analytic coefficient of variance between the two
models is identical (0.200).
I realize there is no "cookbook" method for choosing model fit, but do you
think I should give consideration to the negative exponential model, even
though I don't have any strong reason to believe that the data are truly
spiked? Or should the negative exponential model be avoided in normal
circumstances, as stated in the book?
Last question, are there answers available for the exercises in the book?
Thank you in advance for any help you can give.
Sincerely,
Joe Roberts

messages.subject: Re: zero encounter rate, use of neg exponential model
messages.subject_clean: zero encounter rate, use of neg exponential model
messages.body_plain:
Hi Joe, list,

The reason that we advise against the negative exponential model is that it is
implausible for most studies, having no "shoulder" at the transect line.  In other
words, if probability of detection is 1.0 on the line, under the negative
exponential it is less than 1.0 just off the line.  It is hard to see how this can
happen in most studies -- if it's 1.0 then it's likely to be 1.0 for some (albeit
small) distance away from the line.  Indeed, as we say in the book, using survey
methods that maximize the width of this "shoulder" is one of the keys to reliable
abundance estimation in distance sampling.

As figure 2.5 in the book shows, you don't need an extraordinary spike near 0
distance for the negative exponential model to fit the data quite well -- although
those data are in intervals and hopefully yours were measured as exact distances.
In the latter case, try getting Distance to produce histograms with lots of cut
points in close to the line (in Model Definition | Detection Function |
Diagnostics) and look for evidence of a shoulder, and also of possible violation
of assumptions.  If you have a spike at 0 it may be due to rounding.  If you have
lots of observations close to zero (more than you would expect under a model with
a shoulder) it may be evidence of movement towards the observer or perhaps a
composite detection function (e.g., Figure 2.1 in the book).  When there are any
"problems" of this sort, AIC is not a reliable guide as to which detection
function to use.

As for answers to exercises, I don't think there are any I'm afraid.  I'm cc'ing
this to David Borchers, who I think wrote the exercises in case I'm wrong he can
correct me.

Hope this helps,

 - Len Thomas

--
Len Thomas, Co-ordinator, Distance Development Project
Research Unit for Wildlife Population Assessment
Centre for Research into Environmental and Ecological Modelling
The Observatory, University of St Andrews, Scotland KY16 9LZ

             email: dist...@mcs.st-and.ac.uk
Distance home page: http://www.ruwpa.st-and.ac.uk/distance/

Distance is sponsored by the Wildlife Conservation Society: http://wcs.org

for an MSc.   My problem arises when trying to analyse data from open =
plains habitat.  Visibility is large and observations are probably =
restricted more by topography than visibility in the habitat.  My data =
lacks any real 'shoulder' and peaks and troughs occur throughout.  I =
have truncated the largest 10% of observations but regardless of which =
model I try to fit the result is always a straight line!  I don't really =
want to truncate much more of the data because I don't believe the =
observations were spurious.  Should I even be trying to use DISTANCE for =
these analyses?  and if so should I be truncating more of the data =
(bearing in mind this will seriously reduce my number of obs)?  Which is =
the best model to apply? =20

justine...@virgin.net

messages.subject: Re: data truncation
messages.body_plain:
> > I am currently trying to analyse data collected in the field last year for an MSc.   My problem arises when trying to analyse data from open plains habitat.  Visibility is large and observations are probably restricted more by topography than visibility in the habitat.  My data lacks any real 'shoulder' and peaks and troughs occur throughout.  I have truncated the largest 10% of observations but regardless of which model I try to fit the result is always a straight line!  I don't really want to truncate much more of the data because I don't believe the observations were spurious.  Should I even be trying to use DISTANCE for these analyses?  and if so should I be truncating more of the data (bearing in mind this will seriously reduce my number of obs)?  Which is the best model to apply?

Why not just use the fitted straight line?  It suggests that you're
detecting just about everything in the strip, so truncating more data
won't help.  If you use the uniform key without adjustments, then you're
carrying out a strip transect analysis, assuming all animals in the strip
were detected.  Distance handles this.

Steve Buckland
